notes.b: Cereals are mostly starch, with some protein, sugar, cellulose and B group vitamins, and heat changes all of them. The way you heat the cereal, with moisture or without, decides which change is most obvious.
points: Moist heat (boiling, simmering, steaming) makes starch granules absorb liquid, swell and burst. This is why the cereal softens and thickens the liquid around it.
Dry heat (baking, roasting, toasting) dries the surface and breaks the starch down into dextrins, a change called dextrinisation. This forms a brown, crisp crust.
In frying, the starch also absorbs fat, so the cooked cereal food takes up fat as well as browning.
Dry heat also caramelises sugars in cereal products (heating sugar until it turns brown), adding colour and flavour.
Heat softens the cellulose (the fibre) in the bran and cell walls, so cooked cereals are easier to digest.
Heat coagulates protein (it sets firm), which sets the structure of batters, doughs, baked goods and cooked cereals.
Heat destroys some B group vitamins, and more are lost when cereals are boiled in a large volume of water that is then discarded, because the vitamins dissolve into it.
Overall, the colour, flavour and texture of the cereal all change during cooking.
notes.tip: When asked to outline effects of heat on cereals, pick distinct effects: starch swelling and bursting in moist heat, dextrinisation, absorbing fat, cellulose softening, protein coagulating, B vitamin loss or caramelising. Keep dextrinisation (starch browning) separate from caramelisation (sugar browning).

notes.b: Gelatinisation is what happens when starch is heated in a liquid: the granules absorb water, swell and burst, and the mixture thickens. It is how flour or cornflour thickens a sauce.
points: 1. Starch granules absorb water from the liquid and swell.
2. Some starch (amylose) leaches out of the swollen granules into the liquid.
3. The liquid thickens as the swollen granules and amylose form a gel-like network that fills it.
4. On further heating the granules burst, and the starch is fully gelatinised.
Heat is essential. Flour left cold in a liquid only forms a paste, so it does not thicken by absorbing liquid alone.
Starch granules must be kept apart before heating, by stirring, by blending the flour with a little cold liquid first, or by rubbing fat in as in a roux. Otherwise they clump into lumps.
Flour or cornflour must be cooked long enough to gelatinise fully, otherwise the sauce tastes floury.
A roux is a cooked mixture of equal weights of fat and flour, used as the base of a sauce. The fat coats the starch granules and keeps the flour from forming lumps when the liquid is added.
notes.tip: Explaining gelatinisation is worth 3 marks in the exam: say the starch is heated with liquid, the granules swell and burst, and the mixture thickens. Do not give a temperature, and remember a roux has equal amounts of fat and flour, so a statement of different amounts is false.

notes.b: Rice shows clearly what moist heat does to a cereal, and the same ideas apply to pasta and oats. The method you choose also decides how many B vitamins you keep.
points: Rinsing rice removes surface starch, so that the cooked grains stay separate instead of sticking together.
Absorption method: rice is cooked in a measured amount of water, covered, until all of the water is absorbed, and it is left off the heat to finish.
Boiling method: rice is cooked in excess water, which is drained off afterwards.
Moist heat makes rice grains swell, burst and absorb liquid, and gelatinisation gives the cooked rice its soft texture.
Fibre in the grain softens during cooking, making the rice easier to digest. Its colour also changes.
B group vitamins leach (dissolve out) into the cooking water, so use only the water needed, cover the pan, do not overcook, and use the cooking liquid, for example in soups, where practical.
Brown rice takes longer to cook than white rice because the intact bran layer slows water absorption into the grain.

Pasta is boiled in plenty of boiling water until al dente (cooked but still slightly firm). Oats for porridge are cooked in milk or water and stirred as the starch gelatinises, which stops lumps forming.
notes.tip: If asked for two effects of cooking on rice, choose from: grains swell, burst and absorb liquid; fibre softens; gelatinisation; some vitamin B is lost; colour changes. Link brown rice's longer cooking time to the bran layer slowing water entry.

notes.b: A raising agent produces or traps a gas (air, steam or carbon dioxide) that expands in the heat of baking. The protein and starch then set around the bubbles and hold the structure, giving a light, risen product.
points: Air (a physical raising agent) is trapped by beating, whisking eggs, creaming fat and sugar, sieving flour, folding and rubbing in. It expands in the oven, as in sponge cakes, meringues and, slightly, shortcrust pastry.
Steam: water in a mixture turns to steam in the hot oven and expands the product, as in choux pastry, puff and rough puff pastry, Yorkshire pudding and pancakes.

Yeast (a biological raising agent) ferments sugars in warm, moist dough, producing carbon dioxide and alcohol and releasing energy. The gluten (a protein, not starch) traps the gas and the dough rises during proving.
Yeast works best at about 35-40 degrees Celsius and is killed above about 55-60 degrees Celsius, so dough is proved in a warm place, not a hot one. Baking then kills the yeast.

Bicarbonate of soda (bread soda) releases carbon dioxide when it reacts with an acid such as buttermilk, yoghurt, treacle or honey in the presence of moisture and heat. It is used in soda bread and scones.

Baking powder contains bicarbonate of soda with an acid salt and a starch filler. The acid and alkali react when moistened and heated to release carbon dioxide, so it is used in cakes, muffins and scones.
Self-raising flour is plain flour with baking powder already added.

Raising agents for named products: bread uses yeast, bread soda, or air or baking powder; sponge cake uses air, self-raising flour or baking powder; muffins use baking powder or bread soda; lemon drizzle cake uses baking powder or air.
notes.tip: When asked for a raising agent for a named product, each agent in your answer must be different. To explain the principle, say yeast ferments sugar to make carbon dioxide and alcohol, or that bread soda needs an acid to react with. Gluten traps gas, it does not make it.

notes.b: A raising agent only works if the mixture and the oven let it do its job. Small errors in measuring or handling can leave a baked product flat or heavy.
points: Measure accurately, because too much or too little raising agent gives a poor rise or a coarse texture.
Use the correct oven temperature, so the gas expands and the protein and starch set at the right moment.
Do not open the oven door early, because the cold air can make the risen mixture collapse before it has set.
Handle the mixture correctly, for example folding gently so the trapped air is not knocked out.

keyTerms.definition: The process in which starch granules absorb water, swell and burst when heated, thickening the liquid.
The breakdown of starch into dextrins by dry heat, which browns the surface of cereal products.
The browning of sugars under dry heat, which produces colour and flavour.
A type of starch that leaches out of swollen granules during gelatinisation and helps thicken a liquid.
The setting of protein by heat, which firms the structure of batters and doughs.
Leaving yeast dough in a warm place so that the yeast ferments and the dough rises.
A substance or process that produces gas or steam to make a baked product light and open in texture.
A chemical raising agent containing bicarbonate of soda, an acid salt and a starch filler.
A cooked mixture of fat and flour used as the base for thickening a sauce.

factCards.term: Two effects of dry heat on cereal products
factCards.definition: Dextrinisation browns and crisps the starch on the surface, and sugars caramelise.
Physical (air and steam), chemical (bicarbonate of soda and baking powder) and biological (yeast).
Granules absorb water and swell; amylose leaches out; the mixture thickens; granules burst on further heating.

Two conditions yeast needs to ferment dough
factCards.definition: Warmth and a supply of sugar and moisture.

questions.prompt: Name a suitable raising agent for a sponge cake and for a loaf of bread, and explain how one of them produces the lift in the product.
questions.model: Sponge cake: air incorporated by whisking, or baking powder. Bread: yeast or bread soda. Explanation, yeast: it ferments sugars in warm, moist dough, producing carbon dioxide; gluten traps the gas, so the dough expands during proving and the gas expands further in the oven. Explanation, bread soda: it reacts with an acid in the presence of moisture and heat to release carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: Discuss the effects of moist and dry heat on cereals, and explain how gelatinisation thickens a white sauce made with flour.
questions.model: Moist heat: starch granules swell, burst and absorb liquid; cellulose softens; B group vitamins may leach into the water; protein coagulates in batters. Dry heat: starch dextrinises and the surface browns; sugars caramelise; the surface crisps; protein sets. Heat in general improves digestibility. Gelatinisation in a white sauce: fat and flour are cooked to form a roux, the liquid is added gradually to avoid lumps, and the mixture is brought to the boil; starch granules absorb water and swell, amylose leaches out, the mixture thickens as the swollen granules fill the liquid, and the granules burst with further heating. The sauce must be cooked long enough for the starch to gelatinise fully, so that it does not taste floury.
